Unsecured Lending

By: Graham Coetzer | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We expose how unscrupulous operators buy your debt from banks, and illegally obtain your personal information and have judgements taken against you

Summary:
For the last three years Cambist has been offering investors the impossible – a 19.5% return guaranteed on their investment by buying up bad debt. It sounded like an offer that was too good to be true but for three years investors have been receiving their repayments on time and without any issues. So has Cambist achieved the impossible? Or is there more going on?
Cambist is part of a spider’s web of partially-connected companies – Bridge, OneLaw, Flemix, Solvo, OneSys to name but a few. Bridge, a similar investment scheme, was placed under business rescue earlier this year and investors were told that if the company is liquidated they’ll only get 18c for every R1 of their original investment. But Cambist has been going to great lengths to stress that they are a separate company to Bridge and are not affected in any way. Then on Monday 1 December, around 300 employees of OneLaw, the company that owns and runs Cambist, got a nasty surprise – the company was being liquidated. There was no warning, there would be no severance packages and everyone had an hour to pack up their desks and leave. But Cambist insists things are still fine and investors will keep getting their money. To put it into perspective Cambist has received approximately R700-million in investments – even former Foreign Minister Pik Botha is an investor.


Further information:
The various rounds of retrenchments have been good for us though – sources are now coming forward and revealing for the first time how Cambist has been able to pay such high returns. Cambist’s model is to buy bad debts from banks – i.e. unsecured loans given to poorer South Africans who can’t afford repayments and go into default – they buy the loans at a 40 percent discount, pay a law firm to trace the debtor and get a garnishee, and then sell the loans on to “investors” (joe public). Many suspected that Cambist was simply a Ponzi scheme (there may be an element of that), but what we have established is that Cambist has been acting illegally by bribing court officials to rush through illegal garnishees and by bribing government officials to obtain confidential data on hundreds of thousands of South Africans. We can show how Cambist bribed officials at the UIF to buy the salary information of every employee of the 1000 biggest companies in South Africa, including SAA, Eskom, KPMG, Vodacom and every government department. Sources also claim that Cambist (OneLaw) forged signatures on garnishees and paid off court employees to rush up to 8000 garnishees every month in order to feed the insatiable appetite of their investors.
With Cambist possibly on the verge of collapse the investors who got such high returns now stand to lose their initial investment. The Aldum Family, the owners and creators of this entire empire, are likely to get off scott-free – according to sources they are in the process of moving their money into trusts and out of the country to Georgia, Russia.

My main source on the story was the person responsible for the illegal intelligence gathering on behalf of Cambist, Onelaw, Bridge etc. We have documentary evidence proving info was illegally obtained from UIF on behalf of Cambist. Our sources will also reveal how they paid officials in certain courts to put through thousands of garnishee orders without following procedure or the correct checks and balances.We are also going to approach Cambist and offer to sell them illegal data on hidden camera.

Script:


Sound Up “Henry”
He asked us to find sources that would sell us whole databases of the government.

Sound Up “Victoria”
We weren’t allowed to talk – er – about it otherwise we would have been dismissed.

Sound Up “Henry”
The end goal was… to get the complete database of every single working person in South Africa.

Sound Up “Robert”
I remember he would come into the office with a big brown envelope with definitely a lot of cash inside.

Sound Up “Henry”
…They mentioned R400 000 that they would pay a person…every four months for this kind of data.

Link Devi
For the past few years an investment scheme in Pretoria called Cambist has been offering an incredible 19.5 percent return on your investment with very low risk – but they were selling what most people don’t want – bad debt.

Sound Up Cambist Video
Introducing the Cambist Online Platform where members of the public can earn an annual return of 19.5% by purchasing good debt contracts.

Voice
Cambist was the brainchild of debt collection guru Corne Aldum and his company Onelaw, who saw a way to make millions off the country’s mountains of bad debt. It’s estimated that more than half of South Africa’s consumers with credit have missed 3 installment payments or more. According to analyst Ilan Stermer, when debts go bad, many banks and retailers, would rather sell the debt than try to recover it.

Sound Up Ilan
“The bank or the retailer will manage the debt, will manage the collection of the debt up to a particular point. If that debt then goes bad, somebody doesn’t make a number of payments, etc., they will take a decision to sell that debt to a collector.”

Voice
Without realizing it, your R5000 personal loan could be bundled up into a debtors’ book and sold on to a debt collector at a hefty discount.


Sound Up Ilan
“Typically a collector would not buy a book for far more than 10 cents in the rand, and they would obviously look to collect on that.

Voice
It may sound like paying R10 for R100 worth of IOUs is a good bargain, but because these are small, unsecured personal loans, it’s often virtually impossible to find the debtor making those debts worthless.

Ilan:
“Look information is vital to this process... you have to find the individual to collect the debt.

Link Devi
But Cambist had a distinct advantage, the kind of advantage you can only get if you don’t play by the rules.

Devi
What was the goal here?

Sound Up Robert
To get as much information, personal information on anybody that might be employed by any company in South Africa.

Voice
“Robert” is one of several people hired by OneLaw to covertly gather confidential information on debtors. Most debt collection companies access information from credit bureaus – but the information is often outdated.

Sound Up “John”
Devi: So what are some of the places they would have bought information from?
John: They would have bought information from UIF, anywhere they can get their hands on data they will buy it.
Devi: Is that legal?
John: Uh, it’s not legal no.

Voice
According to numerous sources, OneLaw wanted the most up-to-date information they could get, even if they had to acquire it illegally.

Sound Up “Henry”
Some of the sources we got to work for us worked in government departments where they helped us to get information on companies.

Sound Up “Robert”
We used the money again that was supplied to us by Onelaw to obviously bribe them and convince them to supply information.

Sound Up Devi
Was bribe money easily available?
“Robert”
Yes. You just ask and say listen I’ve got this amount of information.

Devi
So how much would you pay for good data?
“Henry”
25c per id… if you collect a lot of data, where 10,000, 20,000, 30,000 people and you multiply that by 0.25 cents in the rand then it adds up to a lot of money.

Devi
So how did they get the databases to you?
“Robert”
They’ll put it on a memory stick and we’ll meet at a place and they’ll hand it over to us.

Voice
At first the idea was that these employees would only track down debtors, people who owed money and weren’t paying.

Link Devi:
But at some point that was not enough. Onelaw had big dreams – they’d set their sights on collecting the data on every single employed South African.

Voice
Insiders say OneLaw’s ambition was to build their own database stocked with stolen personal information from the UIF. Not only would this make tracing debtors faster, but this would help the company to more accurately analyse risky debtors’ books, giving them a huge advantage over their competitiors.

Sound Up “Henry”
They mentioned R400,000 that they would pay a person… every four months for this kind of data. So that it could be live data.

Voice
Corne Aldum declined an on camera interview with Carte Blanche, but in a written response he denies procuring the UIF database or any other data illegally, saying Onelaw only obtained data from credible third party service providers.

Sound Up “Robert”
Their main priority was to get the full database of the UIF. We were very pushed to get that database.


Voice
In this email from a senior Onelaw manager to one of the staff tasked with gathering data, the manager asks if it would be possible to buy information on every company in South Africa. OneLaw went into liquidation before they could buy the whole database, they were still able to buy the personal details of every single employee - from the cleaners right up to the CEO – of major companies including banks, auditing firms, mining companies, and government departments.

Sound Up “Henry”
At one stage, the company’s database was almost 4-million working people.

Link Devi
But the data wasn’t all – they needed to collect on the debts. But how do they do that? Garnishee orders.

Voice
A garnishee order or emolument attachment order is a court order that instructs an employer to deduct money from an employee’s salary to repay a debt that they owe. It’s the most secure way to collect on a debt, but a 2008 study by the University of Pretoria showed numerous instances of abuse in the system.

Sound Up “Henry”
There were people paid at Magistrate’s offices that worked at the clerk of the court. That used to help to get these papers through in a court so that the garnishees could be issued.

Voice
Corne Aldum says Onelaw staff never paid clerks of the court to expedite garnishee orders, but that’s not what insiders told us.

Sound Up “Victoria”
At that stage we were using one court. That was Kempton Park court, and the Clerk of the Court processed them quickly and got paid for processing our documents quickly.

Voice
A garnishee order is supposed to be issued by the court where the debtor is employed. But in many cases, while the debtor might be a mine worker in Rustenberg, the attorneys acting for OneLaw would apply for a garnishee in a completely different part of the country.

Sound Up Clark Gardner
The constitutional right to access justice to defend your situation has been removed.

Voice
Clark Gardner runs Summit. They review garnishee orders for big companies to make sure that the garnishees are valid and that their employees aren’t being overcharged for interest and legal fees. Clark says garnishee abuse is costing the country millions.

Sound Up Clark
We’re talking about 2, 3-billion rand being stolen from a group of South Africans that cannot afford to be stolen from.

Voice
Clark says he has repeatedly identified problems with the ways in which OneLaw’s attorneys, usually a company called Flemix and Associates, obtain garnishees.

Sound Up Clark
At a Magistrate’s Court level, we have applied for recessions, a few against Flemix as well, where the incorrect jurisdiction has been used to obtain the emolument attachment order, and we’ve been successful.

Voice
In a written response to Carte Blanche, Flemix and Associates deny bribing clerks at the court to expedite garnishee orders and say they are within their rights to take judgement against a debtor in a jurisdiction other than where the debtor works if the debtor has consented to the alternative jurisdiction. But Clark disagrees.

Sound Up Clark
You cannot consent to an emolument attachment order, otherwise known as a garnishee order in a different jurisdiction.

Voice
We went to OneLaw’s offices looking for answers, but instead we found their once plush offices empty. We weren’t the only ones looking for OneLaw though.

Devi
So why are you here today?
Prince
I come to clear up my name with these people.

Voice
Prince Moagi is one of many South Africans who had their salaries garnisheed by Flemix, the firm of attorneys working for OneLaw. He had taken a R5000 loan from ABSA but when he lost his job he fell behind on payments. When he got a new job, OneLaw’s attorneys turned up at his new employer.

Prince
They said you owe Absa the money then I said yes I do know the money for Absa and I’m willing to pay.

Voice
Despite there being a debit order on his account, OneLaw’s attorneys, Flemix and Associates, went ahead and obtained a garnishee order against him.

Prince
I don’t know why they garnished me because I was paying their money.

Voice
This was a common practice according to sources.

Sound Up “Victoria”
Oom Corne said they must go ahead and go through with the garnishee order even if the guys debit order is going off.

Voice
Corne Aldum has denied giving instructions to obtain garnishee orders when debtors had already agreed to repay loans. Prince was able to get his bank to reverse the double payments, but despite repaying his loan, his name had not been removed from the ITC list. We followed Prince to Flemix’s new offices. Surprised to find Carte Blanche on their doorstep they offered to sort out Prince’s problem.

Sound Up “Henry”
This in my eye was just a way to make millions and get away with it. And the people that actually did the work are suffering.
Voice
In December last year OneLaw announced they were liquidating and retrenched more than 300 of their staff.

Sound Up “Robert”
They just told them, all of them, it’s finish and klaar they can go.

Voice
So where does that leave the investors who sunk their money into Cambist’s 19.5% promise? Corne Aldum says Cambist investors will keep getting their payments. Although if anything goes wrong, OneLaw won’t be there to help.

Link Devi For the past few years an investment scheme in Pretoria called Cambist has been offering an incredible 19.5 percent return on your investment with very low risk – but they were selling what most people don’t want – bad debt. Sound Up Cambist Video Introducing the Cambist Online Platform where members of the public can earn an annual return of 19.5% by purchasing good debt contracts. Voice Cambist was the brainchild of debt collection guru Corne Aldum and his company Onelaw, who saw a way to make millions off the country’s mountains of bad debt. It’s estimated that more than half of South Africa’s consumers with credit have missed 3 installment payments or more. According to analyst Ilan Stermer, when debts go bad, many banks and retailers, would rather sell the debt than try to recover it. Sound Up Ilan “The bank or the retailer will manage the debt, will manage the collection of the debt up to a particular point. If that debt then goes bad, somebody doesn’t make a number of payments, etc., they will take a decision to sell that debt to a collector.” Voice Without realizing it, your R5000 personal loan could be bundled up into a debtors’ book and sold on to a debt collector at a hefty discount. Sound Up Ilan “Typically a collector would not buy a book for far more than 10 cents in the rand, and they would obviously look to collect on that. Voice It may sound like paying R10 for R100 worth of IOUs is a good bargain, but because these are small, unsecured personal loans, it’s often virtually impossible to find the debtor making those debts worthless. Ilan: “Look information is vital to this process... you have to find the individual to collect the debt. Link Devi But Cambist had a distinct advantage, the kind of advantage you can only get if you don’t play by the rules. Devi What was the goal here? Sound Up Robert To get as much information, personal information on anybody that might be employed by any company in South Africa. Voice “Robert” is one of several people hired by OneLaw to covertly gather confidential information on debtors. Most debt collection companies access information from credit bureaus – but the information is often outdated. Sound Up “John” Devi: So what are some of the places they would have bought information from? John: They would have bought information from UIF, anywhere they can get their hands on data they will buy it. Devi: Is that legal? John: Uh, it’s not legal no. Voice According to numerous sources, OneLaw wanted the most up-to-date information they could get, even if they had to acquire it illegally. Sound Up “Henry” Some of the sources we got to work for us worked in government departments where they helped us to get information on companies. Sound Up “Robert” We used the money again that was supplied to us by Onelaw to obviously bribe them and convince them to supply information. Sound Up Devi Was bribe money easily available? “Robert” Yes. You just ask and say listen I’ve got this amount of information. Devi So how much would you pay for good data? “Henry” 25c per id… if you collect a lot of data, where 10,000, 20,000, 30,000 people and you multiply that by 0.25 cents in the rand then it adds up to a lot of money. Devi So how did they get the databases to you? “Robert” They’ll put it on a memory stick and we’ll meet at a place and they’ll hand it over to us. Voice At first the idea was that these employees would only track down debtors, people who owed money and weren’t paying. Link Devi: But at some point that was not enough. Onelaw had big dreams – they’d set their sights on collecting the data on every single employed South African. Voice Insiders say OneLaw’s ambition was to build their own database stocked with stolen personal information from the UIF. Not only would this make tracing debtors faster, but this would help the company to more accurately analyse risky debtors’ books, giving them a huge advantage over their competitiors. Sound Up “Henry” They mentioned R400,000 that they would pay a person… every four months for this kind of data. So that it could be live data. Sound Up “Robert” Their main priority was to get the full database of the UIF. We were very pushed to get that database. Voice In this email from a senior Onelaw manager to one of the staff tasked with gathering data, the manager asks if it would be possible to buy information on every company in South Africa. OneLaw went into liquidation before they could buy the whole database, they were still able to buy the personal details of every single employee - from the cleaners right up to the CEO – of major companies including banks, auditing firms, mining companies, and government departments. Sound Up “Henry” At one stage, the company’s database was almost 4-million working people. Link Devi But the data wasn’t all – they needed to collect on the debts. But how do they do that? Garnishee orders. Voice A garnishee order or emolument attachment order is a court order that instructs an employer to deduct money from an employee’s salary to repay a debt that they owe. It’s the most secure way to collect on a debt, but a 2008 study by the University of Pretoria showed numerous instances of abuse in the system. Sound Up “Henry” There were people paid at Magistrate’s offices that worked at the clerk of the court. That used to help to get these papers through in a court so that the garnishees could be issued. Voice Corne Aldum says Onelaw staff never paid clerks of the court to expedite garnishee orders, but that’s not what insiders told us. Sound Up “Victoria” At that stage we were using one court. That was Kempton Park court, and the Clerk of the Court processed them quickly and got paid for processing our documents quickly. Voice A garnishee order is supposed to be issued by the court where the debtor is employed. But in many cases, while the debtor might be a mine worker in Rustenberg, the attorneys acting for OneLaw would apply for a garnishee in a completely different part of the country. Sound Up Clark Gardner The constitutional right to access justice to defend your situation has been removed. Voice Clark Gardner runs Summit. They review garnishee orders for big companies to make sure that the garnishees are valid and that their employees aren’t being overcharged for interest and legal fees. Clark says garnishee abuse is costing the country millions. Sound Up Clark We’re talking about 2, 3-billion rand being stolen from a group of South Africans that cannot afford to be stolen from. Voice Clark says he has repeatedly identified problems with the ways in which OneLaw’s attorneys, usually a company called Flemix and Associates, obtain garnishees. Sound Up Clark At a Magistrate’s Court level, we have applied for recessions, a few against Flemix as well, where the incorrect jurisdiction has been used to obtain the emolument attachment order, and we’ve been successful. But Clark disagrees. Sound Up Clark You cannot consent to an emolument attachment order, otherwise known as a garnishee order in a different jurisdiction. Voice We went to OneLaw’s offices looking for answers, but instead we found their once plush offices empty. We weren’t the only ones looking for OneLaw though. Devi So why are you here today? Prince I come to clear up my name with these people. Voice Prince Moagi is one of many South Africans who had their salaries garnisheed by Flemix, the firm of attorneys working for OneLaw. Prince They said you owe Absa the money then I said yes I do know the money for Absa and I’m willing to pay. Prince I don’t know why they garnished me because I was paying their money. Voice This was a common practice according to sources. Sound Up “Victoria” Oom Corne said they must go ahead and go through with the garnishee order even if the guys debit order is going off. Sound Up “Robert” They just told them, all of them, it’s finish and klaar they can go. Voice So where does that leave the investors who sunk their money into Cambist’s 19.5% promise? Corne Aldum says Cambist investors will keep getting their payments. Although if anything goes wrong, OneLaw won’t be there to help. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We expose how unscrupulous operators buy your debt from banks, and illegally obtain your personal information and have judgements taken against you
metadata.Summary: For the last three years Cambist has been offering investors the impossible – a 19.5% return guaranteed on their investment by buying up bad debt. It sounded like an offer that was too good to be true but for three years investors have been receiving their repayments on time and without any issues. So has Cambist achieved the impossible? Or is there more going on? Cambist is part of a spider’s web of partially-connected companies – Bridge, OneLaw, Flemix, Solvo, OneSys to name but a few. Bridge, a similar investment scheme, was placed under business rescue earlier this year and investors were told that if the company is liquidated they’ll only get 18c for every R1 of their original investment. But Cambist has been going to great lengths to stress that they are a separate company to Bridge and are not affected in any way. Then on Monday 1 December, around 300 employees of OneLaw, the company that owns and runs Cambist, got a nasty surprise – the company was being liquidated. There was no warning, there would be no severance packages and everyone had an hour to pack up their desks and leave. But Cambist insists things are still fine and investors will keep getting their money. To put it into perspective Cambist has received approximately R700-million in investments – even former Foreign Minister Pik Botha is an investor.
metadata.Further information: The various rounds of retrenchments have been good for us though – sources are now coming forward and revealing for the first time how Cambist has been able to pay such high returns. Cambist’s model is to buy bad debts from banks – i.e. unsecured loans given to poorer South Africans who can’t afford repayments and go into default – they buy the loans at a 40 percent discount, pay a law firm to trace the debtor and get a garnishee, and then sell the loans on to “investors” (joe public). Many suspected that Cambist was simply a Ponzi scheme (there may be an element of that), but what we have established is that Cambist has been acting illegally by bribing court officials to rush through illegal garnishees and by bribing government officials to obtain confidential data on hundreds of thousands of South Africans. We can show how Cambist bribed officials at the UIF to buy the salary information of every employee of the 1000 biggest companies in South Africa, including SAA, Eskom, KPMG, Vodacom and every government department. Sources also claim that Cambist (OneLaw) forged signatures on garnishees and paid off court employees to rush up to 8000 garnishees every month in order to feed the insatiable appetite of their investors. With Cambist possibly on the verge of collapse the investors who got such high returns now stand to lose their initial investment. The Aldum Family, the owners and creators of this entire empire, are likely to get off scott-free – according to sources they are in the process of moving their money into trusts and out of the country to Georgia, Russia. My main source on the story was the person responsible for the illegal intelligence gathering on behalf of Cambist, Onelaw, Bridge etc. We have documentary evidence proving info was illegally obtained from UIF on behalf of Cambist. Our sources will also reveal how they paid officials in certain courts to put through thousands of garnishee orders without following procedure or the correct checks and balances.We are also going to approach Cambist and offer to sell them illegal data on hidden camera.
